title: Pumping Lemma
body:
The tool for proving a language is **not** regular. It is the only one the course gives you,
and it is always used as a [[Proof By Contradiction]].

It never proves a language *is* regular. If a language passes the pumping test that tells you
nothing: the lemma is a one-way implication and the converse is false. Producing a regex or a
[[DFA]] is the only way to prove regularity.

## Statement

> If $L$ is regular, there exists a **pumping length** $p \geq 1$ such that every $w \in L$
> with $|w| \geq p$ can be split $w = xyz$ where
> 1. $|y| > 0$ (the pumped part is non-empty),
> 2. $|xy| \leq p$ (the split happens within the first $p$ symbols),
> 3. $xy^i z \in L$ for **every** $i \geq 0$.

Condition 3 includes $i = 0$, which deletes $y$ entirely. That case is often the easiest
contradiction, so try it first.

## Why it is true

A [[DFA]] for $L$ has some finite number of states; call it $p$. Feed it a string of length
$\geq p$ and it visits $p+1$ states, so by the pigeonhole principle it must revisit one. The
piece of the string consumed between the two visits is $y$: it is a loop. Loop it any number
of times and the machine ends up in the same place, so the result is still accepted.

Condition 2 falls straight out of this: the repeat has to happen within the first $p$ steps,
because that is when the states run out.

The lemma is pigeonhole applied to state diagrams. If you remember that, you can reconstruct
the statement.

## How to use it

It is an adversary game, and losing track of who chooses what is how people fail this
question. You do not get to pick $p$ or the split.

| Step | Who chooses |
|---|---|
| 1. Assume $L$ is regular | you, for contradiction |
| 2. $p$ exists | the adversary, unknown to you |
| 3. Pick $w \in L$ with $|w| \geq p$ | **you**, and make it in terms of $p$ |
| 4. Split $w = xyz$ satisfying 1 and 2 | the adversary |
| 5. Pick an $i$ with $xy^i z \notin L$ | **you** |

You only control steps 3 and 5, so the whole skill is choosing $w$ so that *every* legal split
breaks. Condition 2 is what makes this possible: it pins $y$ inside the first $p$ symbols, so
if you front-load the string with one symbol type, the adversary has no interesting choices.

## Worked example: $L = \{a^n b^n \mid n \geq 0\}$

Assume $L$ is regular with pumping length $p$. Choose $w = a^p b^p$, which is in $L$ and has
length $2p \geq p$.

By condition 2, $|xy| \leq p$, and the first $p$ symbols of $w$ are all `a`. So $x$ and $y$
consist only of `a`s, and by condition 1, $y = a^k$ for some $k > 0$.

Pump with $i = 2$:

$$xy^2z = a^{p+k}b^p$$

Now there are more `a`s than `b`s, so $xy^2z \notin L$. That contradicts condition 3, so $L$
is not regular. $\blacksquare$

The intuition underneath: a finite automaton has no unbounded memory, so it cannot remember
how many `a`s went past. This is the concrete reason [[Finite Automata]] sit below
[[Pushdown Automata]], which get a [[Stack]] and can therefore do exactly this language.

## Other standard non-regular languages

- $\{ww \mid w \in \Sigma^*\}$, and it is not context-free either
- $\{a^n b^n c^n\}$, not context-free either
- palindromes over $\{a,b\}$ (context-free, not regular)
- $\{a^{n^2}\}$ and $\{a^p \mid p \text{ prime}\}$, where the gaps grow too fast

## There is a second one

Context-free languages have their own pumping lemma, splitting $w = uvxyz$ with two pumped
pieces $v$ and $y$ inflated together, $|vxy| \leq p$ and $|vy| > 0$. Same game, same
adversary structure, one more moving part. That is what proves $\{a^n b^n c^n\}$ is not
context-free, since a [[Pushdown Automata|PDA]] has one stack and can only match one pair.

## Core Facts to Know

- The pumping lemma proves a language is **not** regular. It never proves one is.
- Always a [[Proof By Contradiction]].
- Statement: $w = xyz$ with $|y| > 0$, $|xy| \leq p$, and $xy^iz \in L$ for all $i \geq 0$.
- $i = 0$ is legal and means deleting $y$.
- It holds because a DFA with $p$ states must repeat a state on any input of length $\geq p$: pigeonhole.
- The adversary picks $p$ and the split; you pick $w$ and $i$.
- Pick $w$ in terms of $p$, and use $|xy| \leq p$ to force $y$ into a region you control.
- $\{a^nb^n\}$, $\{ww\}$, and palindromes are the standard non-regular examples.
- The context-free version splits $w = uvxyz$ and pumps $v$ and $y$ together.
- Failing to pump proves nothing about regularity; the converse does not hold.
